exercises.instruction: Which task is the best fit for an AI shortcut?

Summarise this week’s meeting notes.
Automatically approve all refund requests without review.
Turn notes into a tidy checklist.

exercises.context: Extract action items.
exercises.explanation: Clear output fields make it workflow-ready.

options: A person reviews before anything important happens
exercises.explanation: Nice. You stay in control of what matters.

options: A saved prompt with blanks you fill in each time
exercises.explanation: Templates save time and keep quality consistent.

exercises.context: Replying to job applicants.
options: Write a warm reply to [Name] about the [Role] role. Status: [Next step]. Keep it under 120 words.

exercises.instruction: Match the slot to what goes in it

exercises.context: Making a template easy to reuse.
exercises.template: Put changing details in ___ so you can swap them quickly.

exercises.context: A reusable meeting recap.
exercises.explanation: Input, audience, format and next steps. A solid recap template.

exercises.instruction: Tap the template line that will cause trouble

segments: Write an email to [Client name].
Topic: [Topic].
Always promise delivery by tomorrow, no matter what.
Tone: professional and warm, under 150 words.
exercises.explanation: Hard-coding a promise into a template creates problems every time it’s reused.

exercises.instruction: Which step makes a workflow safer?
exercises.context: You auto-draft replies to customers.
options: Review each draft before sending, at least for the first few weeks
exercises.explanation: Trust is earned. Review first, automate more later.

exercises.instruction: Templates are best for tasks that are…
exercises.explanation: You’re building real workflows now!

exercises.instruction: Which is safest to paste into a public AI chat?
options: A generic question about writing a cover letter
exercises.explanation: Never share passwords, private data about others, or confidential work info.

exercises.instruction: Match the data to the right action
exercises.explanation: When in doubt, leave it out or anonymise it.

exercises.context: Getting help with a tough work email.
options: Here is the full email thread with names, phone numbers and the contract value…
Help me reply to a client who’s unhappy about a 2-week delay. Keep it apologetic and propose a new date.
exercises.explanation: You can get great help without sharing identifying details.

exercises.context: You need feedback on a customer complaint.
exercises.template: Replace real names with ___ before pasting.
exercises.explanation: Anonymising keeps people’s data safe.

exercises.instruction: Tap the risky part of this prompt

The meeting is about the Q3 marketing plan.
My login is jane@corp.com and my password is Sunny2024!
Keep it under 100 words.
exercises.explanation: Never share credentials with any AI tool.

exercises.context: Ask for help with a team conflict.
exercises.explanation: Describe the situation, not the people.

exercises.instruction: Before using AI with work data, you should…
exercises.explanation: Many workplaces have approved tools and rules.

exercises.instruction: Passwords should be shared with AI tools…
exercises.explanation: Easy one. Never! You’re already safer.

exercises.instruction: Why can AI outputs be biased?

exercises.explanation: Models reflect patterns in their training data, good and bad.

exercises.context: Write a short description of a great nurse.

They stay calm under pressure.
She should always be gentle, as women are naturally better caregivers.

exercises.instruction: Match the situation to the honest choice

exercises.explanation: Honest use means being transparent and responsible.

exercises.instruction: Pick the prompt that reduces bias

exercises.explanation: Explicitly asking for diversity and no stereotypes helps.

exercises.context: Checking a hiring summary written by AI.
exercises.template: Review AI output for ___ before using it in decisions about people.
exercises.explanation: Decisions about people need extra care.

exercises.context: Ask the AI to check itself.
exercises.explanation: AI can help audit its own output, but you still check.

exercises.instruction: Who is responsible for content you publish with AI help?
exercises.explanation: AI is a tool. You own what you share.
Transparency for the win. Great job on Ethics & Safety!

exercises.context: A picture for your bakery’s menu.
options: A rustic sourdough loaf on a wooden board, soft morning window light, close-up food photography

exercises.instruction: Match the keyword to what it controls

exercises.explanation: Style words set the mood instantly.

exercises.context: A poster for a jazz night.
exercises.explanation: Subject, setting, lighting, style. Chef’s kiss.

segments: Empty beach at sunrise
pastel sky, gentle waves
chaotic crowded city traffic
minimal, peaceful photography
exercises.explanation: Contradictory details fight each other in the image.

exercises.instruction: The image has the wrong colours. Best next step?

exercises.instruction: Match the video prompt term to its meaning
exercises.explanation: Video prompts also describe camera motion.

exercises.context: A short clip for a coffee shop ad.
options: Slow zoom in on steam rising from a latte, cosy café background, warm light, 5 seconds
exercises.explanation: Motion, subject, setting, light and length.

exercises.context: You want a vertical clip for a phone story.

exercises.explanation: Aspect ratio matters for where the clip will be shown.

exercises.context: The logo mock-up looks too busy.
exercises.explanation: Keep what works, change what doesn’t.

Soft afternoon light.

Trees and a picnic blanket in the background.

exercises.instruction: Before posting an AI image of a real event, you should…
exercises.explanation: Transparency builds trust and avoids misleading people.

exercises.instruction: What does giving an AI a “role” do?
options: It changes which AI company answers you
It tells the AI whose perspective and expertise to write from
It makes the AI answer faster
exercises.explanation: A role like “Act as a travel agent” frames the voice, vocabulary and priorities of the reply.

exercises.context: You want advice on a tricky job interview question.
options: Act as an experienced hiring manager. How should I answer “What is your biggest weakness?”
exercises.explanation: The role (hiring manager) gives the AI an expert lens, and the task is clear.

exercises.instruction: Which of these is a role?
exercises.explanation: “Act as…” assigns a role. The others are format, audience and deadline details.

exercises.context: You need help planning healthy weekly meals.
exercises.template: Act as a ___ and create a 5-day dinner plan for a busy family.
exercises.explanation: A nutritionist is the expert whose perspective fits meal planning.

exercises.instruction: Match each need to the best role
exercises.explanation: Matching the role to the task gives replies the right expertise and tone.

exercises.context: Get feedback on your short story.
exercises.explanation: Role first, then the task. Clear and kind.

exercises.instruction: Tap the sentence that ignores the role
exercises.context: Act as a friendly kindergarten teacher and explain why the sky is blue.
segments: Great question, little explorer!
Sunlight is made of many colours mixed together.
Rayleigh scattering is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength.
Blue light bounces around the sky the most, so we see blue everywhere!
exercises.explanation: That sentence uses physics jargon no kindergartner would follow. The role asked for a simple, friendly voice.

exercises.context: You want a workout plan.
options: Act as a certified personal trainer. Build me a 3-day beginner workout plan I can do at home with no equipment.

exercises.context: You want to practise a hard conversation with your boss.
exercises.template: ___ my manager so I can practise asking for a raise.
exercises.explanation: “Pretend to be…” sets up a role-play, a powerful way to rehearse.

exercises.instruction: True or false: a role is the only thing a good prompt needs.
exercises.explanation: Roles help, but you also need a task, context and format. More on that next!

exercises.instruction: What is the “task” in a prompt?
options: The exact thing you want the AI to do
exercises.explanation: The task is the action: summarise, draft, compare, brainstorm, explain…

exercises.instruction: Pick the prompt with the clearest task
exercises.context: You have a long article and little time.
options: Summarise this article in 5 bullet points for someone with 2 minutes.
exercises.explanation: “Summarise” is a clear verb, and the details make the goal concrete.

exercises.instruction: Which word makes the strongest task verb?
exercises.explanation: Action verbs like compare, draft, list or explain tell the AI exactly what to do.

exercises.instruction: Match the verb to its result
exercises.explanation: Picking the right verb is half of a good task.

exercises.context: You can’t decide between two phones.
exercises.template: ___ the Pixel and the iPhone on battery, camera and price.
exercises.explanation: “Compare” sets up a side-by-side answer on the points you care about.

exercises.context: Get party theme ideas.
exercises.explanation: Verb, quantity and situation make a crisp task.

exercises.instruction: Which prompt asks for ONE clear task?

options: Write the agenda, also book a room, also what’s a good lunch, also motivate me
Draft a 30-minute agenda for a project kickoff meeting with 5 people.
exercises.explanation: One clear task per prompt usually gets better results. Chain extra tasks afterwards.

exercises.instruction: Tap the sentence that doesn’t do the task

segments: 1. Keep a consistent bedtime, even on weekends.

3. Keep your bedroom cool and dark.

exercises.template: ___ this email so it sounds warmer but still professional.
exercises.explanation: “Rewrite” keeps your meaning while changing the wording.

exercises.instruction: “Explain photosynthesis simply.” What is the task verb?
exercises.explanation: Nice! “Explain” is the action you’re asking for.

exercises.instruction: Why add context to a prompt?
options: AI can’t read your mind, so background makes the answer fit you
It makes the prompt look longer
AI charges less for long prompts
exercises.explanation: Who it’s for, why, and any constraints turn a generic answer into a useful one.

exercises.context: You want dinner ideas.
options: Give me 5 dinner ideas. I’m vegetarian, have 20 minutes, and only a microwave and a kettle.

options: My dad is 60, loves gardening, budget $50
exercises.explanation: The recipient, interests and budget are what shape good gift ideas.

exercises.context: You’re explaining your job to kids on career day.
exercises.template: Explain what a data analyst does ___.
exercises.explanation: Naming the audience changes vocabulary and examples.

exercises.context: Plan a weekend trip.
exercises.explanation: Destination, group size and budget give the AI what it needs.

Tofu scramble with spinach takes about 10 minutes.
Greek yogurt with honey is another great option.
A peanut butter banana smoothie works on busy days.
exercises.explanation: Greek yogurt and honey aren’t vegan. Always check the reply respects your context.

options: Write a cover letter for a junior UX designer role at a nonprofit. I have 1 year of freelance experience and care about accessibility.
Write a cover letter, make it good.
exercises.explanation: Role, employer type, experience and values make the letter personal.

exercises.context: You’re about to paste meeting notes.
exercises.template: ___ Below are my notes from today’s meeting. Turn them into action items.
exercises.explanation: Labelling pasted material helps the AI separate instructions from content.

exercises.instruction: “For a beginner” is an example of…
exercises.explanation: Exactly. Audience context helps the AI pitch its answer.

exercises.instruction: What does “format” mean in a prompt?
options: The shape of the answer: list, table, email, length
exercises.explanation: Asking for a specific format saves you from re-editing the reply.

exercises.context: You’re comparing three laptops.
options: Compare these 3 laptops in a table with columns for price, weight, battery life and best for.
exercises.explanation: A table with named columns is perfect for side-by-side comparisons.

exercises.instruction: Match the need to the best format
exercises.explanation: The right format makes the answer instantly usable.

exercises.context: You want something you can read in the lift.
exercises.template: Summarise this report in ___.
exercises.explanation: Length limits are format instructions too.

exercises.context: Get a packing checklist.
exercises.explanation: Task, topic and format in one tidy sentence.

exercises.instruction: Which phrase sets tone, a kind of format?
exercises.explanation: Tone is part of how the answer should look and feel.

• Work in 25-minute blocks.
• Focus is a complex cognitive state shaped by sleep, nutrition, environment and motivation, so it’s worth reflecting on all of these factors in depth.
• Take short walking breaks.
exercises.explanation: That bullet is way over 10 words, and there are 4 bullets instead of 3!

exercises.instruction: Which prompt gets a reply you could paste straight into Slack?

options: Write a 2-sentence Slack message announcing team lunch Friday at 12:30, friendly tone, one emoji max.
exercises.explanation: Length, channel, tone and emoji rule leave nothing to guess.

exercises.context: You want to import the answer into a spreadsheet.
exercises.template: List 10 popular houseplants with their light needs ___.
exercises.explanation: Asking for CSV makes the output machine-friendly.
You’ve got it. Short, clear format rules work wonders.

exercises.instruction: The first reply isn’t quite right. Best next move?
options: Reply with specific feedback on what to change
exercises.explanation: AI chats are conversations. Specific follow-ups get you there fast.

exercises.context: The AI wrote a birthday message that’s too long and formal.
options: Shorter and more playful please: max 2 sentences, and mention her love of karaoke.
exercises.explanation: Say what to change and how. Length, tone, and a personal detail.

exercises.context: You like idea #3 from a brainstorm.

exercises.explanation: Building on a good part of the reply is classic iteration.

exercises.context: The AI’s blog intro is boring.
exercises.explanation: Clear fix plus a constraint. Perfect follow-up.

exercises.instruction: When might you start a fresh chat instead of iterating?
options: When the conversation has drifted far off-topic
exercises.explanation: Long, tangled chats can confuse the AI. A clean start with a better prompt helps.

exercises.context: Four follow-ups to an AI-written product description:
segments: “Make it 30% shorter.”
“Add one line about the 2-year warranty.”
“Make it better.”
“Use a confident, upbeat tone.”
exercises.explanation: “Better” how? Specific feedback gets specific improvements.

options: I have bad knees. Replace running with low-impact cardio like cycling or swimming, and keep the rest.
exercises.explanation: Add the missing context, say what to swap, and what to keep.

exercises.context: You want the AI to help improve your own prompt.
exercises.template: Before answering, ask me ___ questions that would help you do this better.
exercises.explanation: Inviting the AI to ask questions is a power move for tricky tasks.

exercises.instruction: Role, task, context, format, iterate. Which one means “refine the reply”?
exercises.explanation: Unit complete energy! You now know all five building blocks.

options: A rule the answer must follow, like length or budget
exercises.explanation: Constraints narrow the answer to what you can actually use.

exercises.context: You want a date-night idea.
options: 3 date-night ideas at home, under $30, no cooking, ready in 1 hour
exercises.explanation: Budget, location, effort and time all filter the ideas.

exercises.instruction: Match the constraint to its type
exercises.explanation: Mix and match constraints to shape answers.

exercises.context: Your audience hates corporate speak.
exercises.template: Explain our new policy in plain English, ___.
exercises.explanation: “No jargon” is a style constraint that keeps it readable.

exercises.context: A quick team-building game.
exercises.explanation: Two clear constraints: time and props.

exercises.instruction: Tap the idea that breaks a constraint

segments: Visit a public park and have a picnic.
Explore the free modern art museum on Sunday.
Book a $90 hot-air balloon ride at sunrise.
Join a free walking tour (tips optional).

exercises.instruction: Which prompt has the most useful constraints?

exercises.context: You only want the answer, not an essay.

options: Make the task impossible or contradictory

options: So the AI picks the right words, depth and examples
exercises.explanation: A CEO and a 7-year-old need very different explanations.

exercises.context: Explain inflation.
options: Explain inflation to a 12-year-old using an example about the price of pizza.
exercises.explanation: Audience plus a relatable example equals clarity.
Tone should fit who’s reading.

exercises.context: A customer’s order arrived broken.
exercises.template: Write a reply to this customer in an ___ tone, offering a free replacement.
exercises.explanation: Empathy first turns a complaint into loyalty.

exercises.context: Introduce yourself to a new team.
exercises.explanation: Tone, audience and length all set.

exercises.instruction: Tap the sentence with the wrong tone

segments: Hi Sam, I hope your week is going well.
Just a friendly nudge that invoice #204 was due last Monday.
Pay immediately or face consequences.
Let me know if you have any questions. Thanks so much!
exercises.explanation: That line is a threat, not a gentle reminder.

exercises.instruction: Which prompt fits a busy executive?
exercises.context: Share project status upward.
options: Write a detailed 2-page narrative of everything we did this month.
Summarise our project status in 3 bullets: progress, risks, decision needed. Executive tone.
exercises.explanation: Executives want the headline, risks and the ask.

exercises.context: Your gran is new to smartphones.
exercises.template: Explain how to video-call me, step by step, ___.
exercises.explanation: Naming her experience level keeps steps simple and kind.
Right. And that changes how persuasive and precise the reply gets.

exercises.instruction: Why include an example in your prompt?
options: It shows the AI the exact style or pattern you want
exercises.explanation: Examples (“few-shot prompting”) are one of the fastest ways to get consistent output.

exercises.context: You need product names for a candle brand.
options: Give me 10 candle names in this style: “Rainy Library”, “Sunday Pancakes”, “Cabin at Dusk”.
exercises.explanation: The examples show the cosy, place-and-moment naming style.

exercises.instruction: Match the term to its meaning
exercises.explanation: More examples usually mean more consistent results.

exercises.context: You want consistent social captions.
exercises.template: Write 5 captions ___: “Monday fuel ☕ — what’s in your cup?”
exercises.explanation: Pointing at an example sets length, emoji use and tone at once.

exercises.context: Turn notes into tidy tasks.
exercises.explanation: A pattern example removes all guesswork.

exercises.instruction: Tap the output that doesn’t follow the example pattern
exercises.context: Example: “Coffee – Energising – $4”. Give 4 more in the same pattern.
segments: Tea – Calming – $3
Smoothie – Refreshing – $6
Hot chocolate is cosy and usually costs around five dollars.
Matcha – Focusing – $5
exercises.explanation: That one ignores the “Item – Feeling – Price” pattern.

exercises.context: Classify customer messages.
options: Classify each message as Billing, Bug or Praise. Examples: “I was charged twice” → Billing. “App crashes on login” → Bug. “Love the update!” → Praise.
exercises.explanation: Labels plus examples teach the AI the categories instantly.

exercises.context: Your example is long and you don’t want it copied word for word.
exercises.template: Match the tone of this example, but ___.
exercises.explanation: Tell the AI what to borrow (tone) and what not to (wording).

exercises.instruction: Giving 3 examples before your request is called…
exercises.explanation: You’re officially specific. Great work finishing this unit!

options: A confident answer that is made up or false
When the AI shows an image
exercises.explanation: AI predicts plausible text, and plausible isn’t always true.

exercises.instruction: Which reply is most likely to contain a hallucination?
options: A very specific quote, page number and book title you’ve never heard of
exercises.explanation: Super-specific citations are a classic hallucination hotspot. Always check them.

exercises.instruction: Match the red flag to why it matters
pairs: AI may be out of date
exercises.explanation: Learn the red flags and you’ll catch most errors.

exercises.context: Tell me about the Eiffel Tower.

It was completed in 1889 for the World’s Fair.
It was originally painted bright green and moved from London in 1902.
It’s one of the most visited monuments in the world.

exercises.context: You want the AI to be honest about uncertainty.
exercises.template: If you’re not sure, ___ instead of guessing.
exercises.explanation: Giving the AI permission to say “I don’t know” reduces made-up answers.

According to a 2019 Harvard study, honey cures 94% of colds within an hour.
Bees visit many flowers to make a spoonful.
exercises.explanation: A precise stat with a big-name source and a miracle result is a strong red flag.

exercises.instruction: Pick the prompt that reduces hallucinations
exercises.context: You’re researching a health topic.
options: Tell me everything about vitamin D.
Explain vitamin D basics. Flag anything uncertain, and tell me which claims I should verify with a doctor or official health site.
exercises.explanation: Asking the AI to flag uncertainty makes verification easier.

exercises.instruction: True or false: if an AI sounds confident, it’s correct.
exercises.explanation: Exactly. Confidence is style, not proof.

exercises.instruction: Best way to verify an important AI claim?
options: Check it against a trusted primary source
Ask the same AI if it’s sure
exercises.explanation: Go to the original: official sites, papers, reputable news.

exercises.instruction: Match the claim to the best source
exercises.explanation: Different claims need different trusted sources.

exercises.context: You need facts for a school report.
options: Write my report on renewable energy.
List 5 key facts about solar energy growth, and for each tell me what kind of source I should check to verify it.
exercises.explanation: Use AI to map the topic, then verify at the source.

exercises.context: Checking a link the AI gave you.
exercises.template: Before citing an AI-provided source, ___.
options: open it and confirm it says what the AI claims
exercises.explanation: Links can be broken, wrong or invented. Read them yourself.

exercises.context: Ask for checkable answers.
exercises.explanation: Ask the AI to help you verify, not replace verification.

exercises.instruction: Tap the claim you should verify first
exercises.context: Summary of a news story an AI gave you:
segments: A new park is opening downtown.
It will include a playground and walking trails.
The mayor said it will cut city crime by exactly 61%.
The opening date has not been announced.
exercises.explanation: A precise, dramatic number attributed to a person needs checking.

options: Opening other sources to check who’s behind a claim
exercises.explanation: Fact-checkers leave the page to see what others say about a source.

exercises.instruction: AI is great for ___ and you are responsible for ___.
options: first drafts and overviews / checking facts
exercises.explanation: That’s the winning partnership. AI drafts, you verify.

exercises.instruction: What does a role in a prompt do?
options: It picks which AI company answers
It sets whose expertise the reply draws on
exercises.explanation: A role such as “Act as a hiring manager” frames the voice and priorities of the reply.

exercises.context: You need a status update for your manager.
options: Write a three-line status update for my manager on the Q3 report: done, next, blocked.
exercises.explanation: The second prompt names the audience, the topic and the format.

exercises.context: You want a short answer you can paste into a chat.
exercises.template: Summarise this report ___.
exercises.explanation: A length limit tells the AI exactly how much to write.

exercises.context: Ask for a meeting agenda.
exercises.explanation: Role, task, context and format: each tile adds one thing the AI needs.

exercises.instruction: Tap the sentence that can't come from the sales table.
exercises.context: Summarise Q3 sales for the board. Use only the attached table.
segments: Q3 revenue was €4.2M, up 6% on Q2.
Growth came mostly from the Nordics.
Analysts expect the market to double by 2028.
Customer churn held at 2.1%.
exercises.explanation: A market forecast can't come from a sales table, so the AI added it.

exercises.instruction: Match each prompt part to what it does
exercises.explanation: Each part answers one question the AI would otherwise guess.

exercises.instruction: Which reply should you check before you use it?
options: Any reply that states a fact
exercises.explanation: Fluent replies can still be wrong, so check every factual claim.

exercises.instruction: Which step must stay with a person?
options: Approving the reply before it is sent
exercises.explanation: Approval stays with a person: they own what gets sent.
Mapping the steps first shows which one must stay with a person.

exercises.instruction: Which order keeps a person in control?
exercises.explanation: Approval comes after the draft and before anything is sent.
